newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Ministers skirt around Africa problems at OAU meet.
newsitem.headline: Ministers skirt around Africa problems at OAU meet.

text.p: Foreign ministers began preparing for an Organisation of African Unity summit expected to debate some of the continent's pressing political issues, but diplomatic sources said their first session on Thursday swept around them.

Sierra Leone, where junior army officers staged a coup against democratically elected President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah last Sunday, and former Zaire, where Laurent Kabila is busy establishing his rule after driving out former president Mobutu Sese Seko, had received scant attention, they said.

"It's not the sort of debate people were expecting on these issues. The first session was very formal, repeating condemnations in the case of the Sierra Leone coup and repeating congratulations in the case of the new Democratic Republic of Congo," a Zimbabwean diplomat said.
"Maybe people are still too shocked and still coming to terms with these problems," said one Western diplomat who sat in the closed door meeting as an observer.
Both diplomats declined to be identified.

Real debate on the Great Lakes Region would have involved discussing fears that have been expressed in private by some African leaders that Kabila's victory in former Zaire could be the start of a new chapter in Africa where some countries could openly back the overthrow of neighbouring governments, they said.
Although they have denied it, Rwanda, Burundi, Uganda and Angola are among states that Mobutu's regime accused of militarily backing Kabila's seven-month whirlwind rebel campaign.
Kabila's Foreign Minister Bizima Karaha was expected to join the two-day foreign ministers council which organisers said had began with around 20 ministers from the 53-member body.
Zimbabwe Foreign Affairs Minister Stan Mudenge told reporters the first session had discussed most of the political issues, including the peace efforts in Angola, Somalia and Liberia.
He said the ministers reiterated the OAU's condemnation of the Sierra Leone coup and were looking to the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAs) to help restore constitutional rule.
But Mudenge denied suggestions that Nigeria, which is leading the ECOWAs programme, had been blessed by the OAU to use military force against the coup leaders.
"We never discussed the mechanics," he said.

There has been overwhelming support for Kabbah at preparatory meetings for the June 2-4 OAU summit, but some political analysts say Nigeria seemed to have been using the Sierra Leone issue to win a bigger voice on the African diplomatic stage.

Sierra Leone's U.N. ambassador James Jonah said on Tuesday Kabbah had asked regional states to restore his government and also demanded sanctions against the coup leaders led by Major Johnny Paul Koromah.
